headline: The Neap Takes the Edge Off Fort Trumbull, and the Bass Follow It Down
subhead: Softer current at the river mouth pushed stripers into deeper holding water while bunker-chasing blues took over the surface show.
body_markdown:
The first thing I noticed this week wasn't a fish — it was the water itself. Fort Trumbull on the ebb usually has that hard, defined seam where the river current meets the harbor swing, a visible crease you can read from forty yards off. This week, with the moon sitting on first quarter and the tides going neap, that seam went soft. Still there, still pushing bait, but with none of the teeth it has on a big spring tide. That tells you everything about where the fish have gone and why.

When the rip loses its punch, stripers stop holding right on the current edge and slide down into the deeper holding water — 20 to 25 feet off the Fort Trumbull point, tight to the riprap, and out along the deeper channel edge toward the Gold Star Bridge pilings in 30 to 35 feet. That's where I found them this week, and it's a pattern I've watched repeat every neap cycle for two decades on this river. The bite isn't gone, it's just relocated and it's compressed into shorter windows — first hour of light and the last hour before dark, with the best of it coming after the sun's fully down. Bunker schools have been thick in the upper harbor and pushing into the river mouth on the last of the incoming, and that's pulling bass up out of the channel to feed. Eels fished on a light three-way rig, and 6-inch paddletail swimbaits in bunker colors worked slow along bottom, have been the ticket after dark. Nothing gaudy — slow, deliberate presentations right on the bottom where the current still has some shape to it even on a soft tide.

The bluefish have been the more visible story, and we flagged this coming — bunker moving the coast, blues following, and that's exactly what's happening at our end of the Sound. Ocean Beach and Pleasure Beach have both had morning surface chop from blues working bunker pods right off the sand, close enough to see from the boardwalk on a calm morning. These aren't monster blues, mostly 3 to 5 pounds, but there are numbers of them and they're aggressive. Metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — fished on wire leader has been more than enough. If you see the bunker balled up and nervous, don't overthink it, just get a lure in the water before the school moves. They don't sit still long, especially with harbor traffic pushing through this time of year.

Porgies have been the dependable, unglamorous bread-and-butter option, and with the neap tide slowing everything else down, that steadiness matters. Gold Star Bridge pilings in 25 to 35 feet, and the humps up around the state pier, have been holding good numbers of scup in the 10 to 12 inch range, with the occasional 14-incher mixed in. Sandworms and clam on a simple high-low rig, fished right on bottom on the slower stages of the tide, has been steady work — not exciting, but it fills a cooler when the bigger stuff is playing hard to get. Water temp readings for the Sound put New London around 69 degrees, a touch cooler than the western Sound pushing 71, and that gradient matters more than people think — it's part of why our porgy and bass action stays a notch behind Western Sound reports you might be hearing about. Cooler water, later peak.

Hickory shad, worth mentioning only because people ask — that spring run through the upper Thames wound down weeks ago. If you're still working the shad darts up by the old dam pools expecting river action, you're behind the calendar. That fishery's done until next April. Blackfish are a similar story right now — most guys aren't targeting tog seriously yet this time of year, and the smart money is waiting for that fall push when water starts cooling again and they group up tight on structure. Not worth burning bait on them in July.

Looking ahead, this neap cycle runs a few more days before the tides start building back toward the next spring cycle. That means Fort Trumbull and the bridge pilings should keep fishing on this same soft-current, low-light pattern through midweek — work dawn, dusk, and after dark, target the deeper holding water rather than the rip line itself, and be patient with your retrieve. Once the tides build back up, I expect that current seam at Fort Trumbull to sharpen back up and pull bass back onto the edge where they'll feed more aggressively and through a longer window, including some daylight opportunity again. If the bunker stay thick in the harbor through that transition, and there's no reason right now to think they won't, the bluefish should keep pace right along the beach. I'd plan around the tide change first, the bunker second, and worry about everything else after that.
